title: Ohm's Law
notes: Ohm's law says that the current through a metallic conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature and other physical conditions stay constant. The constant of proportionality is 1/R.
The working form is V = IR. R is the resistance. A steeper I–V line means a smaller resistance if I is plotted vertically, because the slope is 1/R.

The law is empirical for ohmic materials. A filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so its I–V graph curves. A semiconductor diode conducts very differently in the two directions and is non-ohmic.
Resistivity ρ is the material property in R = ρL/A. Ohm's law can hold while R still changes if the piece is stretched, because L and A change.
The ohm is the resistance that passes 1 A when 1 V is applied. Power in a resistor is I^2 R, or V^2/R, or V I, and that power becomes heat.
A circuit calculation uses Ohm's law on each ohmic element after the currents have been chosen. It is not a law of the battery's internal chemistry.
confusion: ❌ 'Ohm's Law applies to all conductors.' ✅ It is valid only for *ohmic conductors* (where V is proportional to I, like metallic resistors), not for non-ohmic devices like diodes or transistors.
❌ 'Ohm's Law defines Resistance (R=V/I).' ✅ Resistance is a *property* of the conductor (geometry/material); Ohm's law states that *for some materials*, R remains constant regardless of V or I.
❌ 'V is always proportional to I.' ✅ This holds true only when *temperature and other physical conditions* are kept constant.
Ohm's law is not true for every device.
The temperature condition is part of the statement.
Slope of I against V is 1/R, not R, in that plotting choice.
